title: US Stocks Are Predicted to Extend Their Historic Rally as Gains Moderate
summary: Goldman Sachs Research forecasts an 18% total return for the S&P 500 through the end of 2027.
body_markdown:
-


Goldman Sachs Research forecasts an S&P 500 total return of 18% through the end of 2027.


-


Earnings growth for the S&P 500 is expected to slow to 11% in 2027 from roughly 30% this year.


-


Our strategists expect earnings, rather than valuations, to continue to drive US equity performance in 2027.


-


Key equity themes for next year include “buyback aristocrats,” companies with secular growth prospects, and stocks with quality attributes such as low volatility and strong balance sheets.


The[S&P 500](https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/markets) has generated triple-digit returns since the start of the bull market four years ago. While US stocks are forecast to climb higher in 2027,[Goldman Sachs Research](https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/goldman-sachs-research) expects US stock returns to moderate as earnings growth slows.


**What is Goldman Sachs Research’s outlook for S&P 500 gains in 2027?**


The S&P 500 is predicted to generate a total return of 18% through the end of 2027 (as of November 17), writes Ben Snider, chief US equity strategist, in the team’s report.Earnings are expected to grow by a robust 11% in 2027, or 18% excluding mega-cap tech “other income” from private investment stakes. However, that is a step down from the roughly 30% growth rate this year, and growth will likely slow further in 2028.


“Positive but decelerating growth has historically been associated with positive but moderating S&P 500 returns as well as rotations within the equity market,” Snider writes. In these environments, returns are typically driven by earnings growth as valuation multiples decline.


US stocks are on pace in 2026 for a fourth-straight year of gains, and the S&P 500 has returned 120% since late 2022. This four-year bull market return ranks as the strongest in the last 50 years outside of the dot-com bubble and the recoveries following recessions, according to Goldman Sachs Research.


What will drive US stock returns in 2027? ****


“AI investment has driven a surge in S&P 500 earnings in 2026, but that tailwind should begin to fade in 2027,” Snider writes. Capital expenditures in artificial intelligence (AI) have produced about half of the S&P 500’s growth in earnings per share this year. That impulse will likely be smaller in 2027 as the growth rate of capex slows and depreciation expenses build, according to Goldman Sachs Research. Earnings growth is also expected to slow modestly in 2027 for companies outside of AI infrastructure.


Even so, Snider expects earnings, rather than valuations, to continue to drive equity returns in 2027. He says elevated interest rates, decelerating earnings growth, and AI-driven uncertainty should prevent broad expansion in multiples, such as price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios, in 2027.


**What are the risks to US stock gains in 2027?**


“The biggest downside risk to equities in 2027 is a deterioration in the earnings outlook for 2028,” Snider writes. **** AI investment growth will likely remain robust in 2027, as will its contribution to S&P 500 earnings. However, the market is forward looking, and that theme could play out in a broad range of ways in 2028. In addition to uncertainty around AI investment spending in 2028, the potential for rising semiconductor supply threatens profit margins and earnings, according to Goldman Sachs Research.


Our strategists estimate that each $50 billion of AI capex, or 1 percentage point change in semiconductor profit margins, in 2028 would shift S&P 500 earnings-per-share (EPS) growth by about 1 percentage point. If consensus S&P 500 EPS estimates fell back to the 30-year trend and the P/E ratio fell to the 30-year average of 17x, the S&P 500 would decline by roughly 25% to a level of approximately 5,600.


In addition, S&P earnings growth and recent stock returns have been highly concentrated in a handful of stocks. As the earnings growth from the AI investment cycle fades, the key question is whether another sufficiently large source of earnings strength will emerge to sustain index-level profits, Snider writes. Some of the dynamics during the late stages of other bull markets—such as Federal Reserve rate hikes—are taking place today.


“One striking contrast with past overextended bull markets is the lack of speculative mania in today’s market,” Snider notes. He points out that recent equity returns have generally tracked near-term earnings outlooks. While active fund managers faced a difficult backdrop in much of 2026, Snider says earnings-driven returns, elevated dispersion, and improving equity market breadth bode well for stock pickers heading into the new year.


**What themes are expected to drive US stocks in 2027?**


As AI capex decelerates, Snider expects investors to shift their focus to “the next earnings beneficiaries of the AI boom.” For example,cloud-operating hyperscalers have increasingly shown signs of monetization of their AI investments.


Another theme in 2027 may reflect the surge in corporate borrowing that has taken place to fund AI investment. Strong capex has come in part at the expense of buybacks, according to Goldman Sachs Research. That may create opportunities in “buyback aristocrats”—stocks with strong free cash flow generation and a commitment to returning cash to shareholders.


During the past few decades, periods of slowing earnings and economic growth have favored stocks with price momentum, upward earnings revisions, and "quality" attributes such as low volatility and strong balance sheets, Snider writes. He says the information technology and healthcare sectors have a history of outperformance in these situations.


Investors may also benefit from diversifying into defensive stocks, such as consumer staples companies, that tend to deliver stable profits even when the economy slows, according to Snider. “Although our base case is for continued earnings growth and equity market appreciation, the downside risks associated with extended earnings and valuations argue for diversifying portfolios with select defensives,” he writes.
